parts.title: Passage 1 · Getting Started with E-mail!
parts.instructions: Follow the original instructions on the book pages. Questions 1–6: match words with definitions A–F. Questions 7–14: classify events using A (1960s), B (1970s), C (1980s) or D (1990s). Questions 15–19: choose A, B, C or D.

questions.prompt: Match transmit with its definition.
questions.explanation: Transmit means to send something from one person or place to another. In this passage, computers send messages electronically.
questions.evidence: E-mail is a way of sending a message from one computer to one or more other computers around the world.

questions.prompt: Match numerous with its definition.
questions.explanation: Numerous means many. The message pieces can travel along many routes before reaching their destination.
questions.evidence: The pieces might travel numerous routes through other computers on the way.

questions.prompt: Match academic with its definition.
questions.explanation: Here academic is a noun referring to a university or college teacher or researcher. A member of a college or university is the matching definition.
questions.evidence: academics in a number of fields were using e-mail for professional collaboration

questions.prompt: Match military with its definition.
questions.explanation: Military means relating to armies or the armed forces. The passage describes military officials and the U.S. military.
questions.evidence: Military officials were looking for a way that communications could be carried out

questions.prompt: Match tiny with its definition.
questions.explanation: Tiny means very small. The computer breaks the message into very small pieces for transmission.
questions.evidence: break the message up into tiny pieces

questions.prompt: Match reliable with its definition.
questions.explanation: Reliable means dependable: something that can be trusted to work properly. The officials wanted a system that would continue working if central institutions were destroyed.
questions.evidence: They needed a system that would be very decentralised, reliable, and fast

questions.prompt: Classify the decade: E-mail had a very limited usage in military-related areas.
questions.explanation: The passage places this limited military-related use in the early 1970s. In the exercise, B represents the 1970s.
questions.evidence: Through the early 1970s, e-mail was limited to the U.S. military, defense contractors, and universities doing defense research.

questions.prompt: Classify the decade: People tried to figure out a way of communication if central institutions were ruined.
questions.explanation: According to the passage, officials sought this resilient communication system when e-mail began in the late 1960s. A represents the 1960s.
questions.evidence: Electronic mail (e-mail) was started in the late 1960s ... in case central institutions were destroyed.

questions.prompt: Classify the decade: About 3,000 or 4,000 people were using e-mail.
questions.explanation: The passage says that a few thousand people used e-mail in 1980. This places the event in the 1980s, represented by C.
questions.evidence: A few thousand people were using e-mail in 1980

questions.prompt: Classify the decade: More professors in different universities started to use e-mail.
questions.explanation: E-mail spread more broadly through university communities in the 1970s. This is earlier than the specific professional collaboration described for the 1980s.
questions.evidence: By the 1970s, it had begun to spread more broadly within university communities.

questions.prompt: Classify the decade: Officials in army forces were seeking for a way to communicate in war-time.
questions.explanation: The first paragraph connects the officials’ search for wartime communication with the late 1960s. A is the 1960s in the classification list.
questions.evidence: Electronic mail (e-mail) was started in the late 1960s ... Military officials were looking for a way that communications could be carried out in the event of a large-scale nuclear war.

questions.prompt: Classify the decade: E-mail was widely used for personal information exchanges.
questions.explanation: The passage says personal uses expanded in the early 1990s. The classification letter for the 1990s is D.
questions.evidence: The early 1990s saw an explosion ... for a wide range of professional, academic, and personal purposes.

questions.prompt: Classify the decade: University professors used e-mail for professional cooperation in certain areas.
questions.explanation: Professional cooperation paraphrases professional collaboration. The passage explicitly places academics’ use for this purpose in the 1980s.
questions.evidence: By the 1980s, academics in a number of fields were using e-mail for professional collaboration.

questions.prompt: Classify the decade: Millions of people in the world were using e-mail.
questions.explanation: The estimate of more than 25 million users refers to the mid-1990s, so D is correct.
questions.evidence: more than 25 million people throughout the world were using it in the mid-1990s

questions.prompt: Which step may NOT be correct when you write an e-mail message?
questions.explanation: B reverses the direction of the transfer. The passage allows writing in a word-processing program and then uploading into e-mail software; it does not tell users to upload a message from Pine into a word processor.
questions.evidence: either directly in a special e-mail software program ... or first in a word-processing program, and then transferring (uploading) it into the e-mail software

questions.prompt: When you press a button to send the message, what happens to it?
questions.explanation: The connected computer breaks the message into small pieces. The receiving computer later reassembles the pieces, which is the process described by B.
questions.evidence: break the message up into tiny pieces ... the receiving computer will reassemble them into a message

questions.prompt: How many parts is an e-mail message mainly composed of?
questions.explanation: The text identifies two main parts: the heading and the body. The choice giving Two is D.
questions.evidence: Normally the message would come in two parts: the heading and the body.

questions.prompt: What advantage stated in the passage does e-mail have over fax?
questions.explanation: The comparison table marks e-mail, but not fax, as allowing transmission to one or many people. Speed and a large quantity of information are available for both.
questions.evidence: A major advantage of e-mail is that it allows one message to be sent to hundreds or even thousands of people

questions.prompt: To apply for Internet access to your university, what should your plan be based on?
questions.explanation: The final paragraph recommends a concrete plan based on information in books and discussion with other people. Discussion with other people is the matching printed choice.
questions.evidence: Present a concrete plan ... based on information in books and discussion with other people

parts.title: Passage 2 · Educating Our Mobile Children
parts.instructions: Follow the original instructions on the book pages. Questions 1–6: match words with definitions A–F. Questions 7–11: choose phrases A–H. Questions 12–21: complete the summary using words or phrases from the printed word box.

questions.prompt: Match assumption with its definition.
questions.explanation: An assumption is something accepted as a fact without proof. The experts warn parents not to make unsupported assumptions about their children’s education.
questions.evidence: caution parents against making assumptions about their children’s education

questions.prompt: Match candidly with its definition.
questions.explanation: Candidly means in a sincerely honest and direct way. It describes how the two experts discuss parents’ concerns.
questions.evidence: spoke candidly about some of the common concerns parents have

questions.prompt: Match alternate with its definition.
questions.explanation: To alternate is to switch between things or cause them to follow one another in turn. The passage discusses alternating a child’s school system.
questions.evidence: Parents may be tempted to alternate their children’s school system

questions.prompt: Match domestic with its definition.
questions.explanation: Domestic means of or relating to one’s own country. The passage contrasts students in domestic schools with those in international schools.
questions.evidence: Unlike some students in domestic schools, students in international schools have a stronger sense of empathy

questions.prompt: Match enhance with its definition.
questions.explanation: Enhance means improve or increase a quality. Here the quality is cross-cultural understanding.
questions.evidence: in order to enhance cross-cultural understanding

questions.prompt: Match considerable with its definition.
questions.explanation: Considerable means fairly large in amount or degree. It describes the benefits offered by international school systems.
questions.evidence: The international school systems offer considerable benefits to the mobile child.

questions.prompt: Most families moving overseas will worry about what?
questions.explanation: The opening paragraph says that parents are concerned about the schooling available to their child and possible academic disadvantages. C summarises the decisions about their children’s education.
questions.evidence: What schooling will be available to my child? Will my child be disadvantaged academically as a result of this move?

questions.prompt: What is advised for parents who need to make choices for their children’s education?
questions.explanation: The experts advise parents to research schools and think through schooling issues well before a move. D expresses this advance preparation.
questions.evidence: research post schools as far in advance of a move as possible

questions.prompt: What important factor should parents think about?
questions.explanation: Parents should consider the kind of college or university the child will attend after high school. A is the matching phrase.
questions.evidence: One of the primary factors that should be considered is what type of college or university your child will attend after high school.

questions.prompt: What do many experts agree about school systems?
questions.explanation: Experts recommend continuity in one school system during the high school years, rather than alternating between systems. This is the advice in E.
questions.evidence: try to keep the child in one system ... for all of the high school years

questions.prompt: To keep children in one system in high school, parents may have to do what?
questions.explanation: The passage recommends one consistent system but allows that it may be in more than one location. H is the printed phrase representing this qualification.
questions.evidence: try to keep the child in one system (although this may be in more than one location)

questions.prompt: One concern is the possible ________ to children’s education resulting from an international move.
questions.explanation: Disadvantages is the noun from the printed word box that corresponds to parents’ concern that a move may disadvantage their child academically.
questions.evidence: Will my child be disadvantaged academically as a result of this move?

questions.prompt: Experts warn parents against making ________ about their children’s education.
questions.explanation: The passage directly warns parents against making assumptions, which is also the word supplied in the summary’s box.
questions.evidence: Dr. Mannino and Dr. Miller caution parents against making assumptions about their children’s education.

questions.prompt: Parents making an educated choice need to think through ________ in advance.
questions.explanation: Schooling issues is the phrase used in the passage for the matters parents need to consider before choosing a school.
questions.evidence: parents need to think through schooling issues and to research post schools as far in advance of a move as possible

questions.prompt: There are many school choices for children who are ________.
questions.explanation: Internationally mobile describes the children whose families move between countries. The passage says they have many school choices.
questions.evidence: Children who are internationally mobile have many choices of schools to attend.

questions.prompt: Parents will have to make decisions ________ about an appropriate school.
questions.explanation: The original passage calls the school choice an individual decision based on many factors. The summary requires the adverb individually from the word box.
questions.evidence: Which school is appropriate for your child is an individual decision based on many factors.

questions.prompt: Experts advise continuity because of differences in the ________.
questions.explanation: Differences in the order in which subjects are taught can create academic problems when a child changes systems. The exact phrase in the word box is sequencing of curriculum.
questions.evidence: differences in the sequencing of curriculum exist in the high school grades

questions.prompt: Experts suggest not moving children from one ________ to another during high school.
questions.explanation: The passage specifically warns against changing academic systems during high school because their curricula may have different sequences.
questions.evidence: moving your child from one academic system to another during this time can handicap a child academically

questions.prompt: Otherwise children may be academically ________.
questions.explanation: The summary needs the past participle handicapped after may be. It expresses the academic disadvantage described by the verb handicap in the text.
questions.evidence: moving your child from one academic system to another during this time can handicap a child academically

questions.prompt: International school systems ________ mobile children considerably.
questions.explanation: The passage says international school systems offer considerable benefits. The summary uses the verb benefit with school systems as its plural subject.
questions.evidence: The international school systems offer considerable benefits to the mobile child.

questions.prompt: International-school students may ________ more with new students.
questions.explanation: Students at international schools often understand new students’ feelings because they have experienced being new themselves. Empathise is the matching verb from the word box; empathize is the American spelling.
questions.evidence: students in international schools have a stronger sense of empathy for new kids since almost everyone has been new at one time or another
